messages.subject: Learning gain comparison in MIRT
messages.body_plain:
For my master thesis within Educational Science and Technology, I have an experimental design with students divided over a control and an experimental group based on an educational intervention, and all students wrote both a pre- and posttest. Both tests consists of 5 non overlapping questions, drawn randomly from an itembank consisting of all 10 questions. Therefore, all students have answered the same 10 questions, however they differ in whether the question was answered on the pretest or posttest.

My question is: how can I determine the item difficulties and the students' learning gains, and compare these learning gains between the two groups?

messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I'm wondering if mirt can take in already-calibrated item parameter estimates as anchors in order to further calculate person estimates & then latent regression?
Please kindly advise.

many thanks,

Diah

messages.subject: Re: Using anchored item parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi Diah,

Of course. Just edit the starting values PRN, like so:

#simulate data
set.seed(1234)
N <- 1000

# covariates
X1 <- rnorm(N); X2 <- rnorm(N)
covdata <- data.frame(X1, X2)
Theta <- matrix(0.5 * X1 + -1 * X2 + rnorm(N, sd = 0.5))

#items and response data
a <- matrix(1, 20); d <- matrix(rnorm(20))
dat <- simdata(a, d, 1000, itemtype = 'dich', Theta=Theta)

#conditional model using X1 and X2 as predictors of Theta
sv <- mirt(dat, 1, 'Rasch', covdata=covdata, formula = ~ X1 + X2, pars = 'values')

head(sv)
sv$est[1:6] <- FALSE
mod <- mirt(dat, 1, 'Rasch', covdata=covdata, formula = ~ X1 + X2, pars = sv)
head(mod2values(mod))

scores <- fscores(mod)

Phil

messages.body_plain:
The descriptions you provided are marginal estimates of reliability, and generally reflect what functions like empirical_rxx are for. Also, I think the rxx plots are slightly different because these are essentially distribution agnostic in that they don't represent the marginal distribution variability (because there's nothing marginal about them, and represent more conditional reliability as a function of the inverse information rule). In essence, the plots ignore the empirical ability distribution and generally assume the model is correct (whereas empirical rxx estimates from fscores will include this information implicitly).

So, these formula are different at their cores because they include very different pieces of summary statistics, and therefore have slightly different interpretations.

Phil

messages.subject: Difficulty and guessing model
messages.body_plain:
Dear mirt-community,

I try to estimate a Difficulty and guessing model, that means like a 3PL-model but with a fixed slope.
To be sure that everything works fine with the model I first estimated it with the great package "sirt" from Alexander Robitzsch who helped me a lot.

Because I made the experience that sometimes different packages estimate the models different I wanted to try the same thing with mirt.
Unfortunately there are quite huge differences.

I would appreciate it a lot, if anybody could help me with this.
Below is a syntax with a simulated dataset.

Best

Petra

library(mirt)
library(sirt)
library(TAM)
#***
# (1) simulate data
set.seed(785)
library(mvtnorm)
N <- 500
N <- 3000
theta <- mvtnorm::rmvnorm( N,mean=c(0,0), sigma=matrix( c(1.45,.5,.5,1.7) , 2 ,
                                                        2 ))
theta[,2] <- theta[,1]
I <- 10
# 10 items load on the first dimension
p1 <- stats::plogis( outer( theta[,1] , seq( -2 , 2 , len=I ) , "-" ) )
resp1 <- 1 * ( p1 > matrix( stats::runif( N*I ) , nrow=N , ncol=I ) )
# 10 items load on the second dimension
p1 <- stats::plogis( outer( theta[,2] , seq( -2 , 2 , len=I ) , "-" ) )
resp2 <- 1 * ( p1 > matrix( stats::runif( N*I ) , nrow=N , ncol=I ) )
#Combine the two sets of items into one response matrix
resp_t <- cbind(resp1,resp2)
colnames(resp) <- paste("I" , 1:(2*I), sep="")
dat <- resp_t
#**** Schaetzung in sirt
mod1 <- sirt::rasch.mml2( dat , est.c = 1:20  , theta.k = seq(-6,6,len=21) )
summary(mod1)

#**** Schaetzung in mirt
modelxDAT <- "F = 1-20"
pars <- mirt(dat, itemtype='3PL',modelxDAT, pars = 'values')
pars$est[which(pars$name == 'a1')] <- FALSE
pars$value[which(pars$name == 'a1')] <- 1
mod3 <- mirt(dat, itemtype='3PL',modelxDAT, pars = pars)
coef(mod3)
modelxDAT <- "F = 1-20"

model <- 'F = 1-20

mod3 <- mirt(dat, model, itemtype = '3PL')

Hey Phil,

first of all great package, accessible even to dumb economists like me :)

I'm trying to estimate a Confirmatory Multiple Group model with two groups and two latent dimensions. I've done some EFA to establish the pattern of loadings and decided how to assign each item to each of the two factors. I have 30 items in total: the first 6 I want to use as "anchors" since they are the same in the two groups, and the remaining 24 are specific to either group (so they are NA in the other group). My ultimate aim is to assess the level of "skills" in the two groups, and then score the individuals on both dimensions.

I thus set up and run the model in the following way:

model.syntax <- ('
                  EXT = 1-3, 7-12, 14, 15, 18, 19, 21, 23, 24, 26, 28
                  INT = 4-6, 13, 16, 17, 20, 22, 25, 27, 29, 30
                  CONSTRAINB = (1-3, a1), (4-6, a2), (1-6, d), (7-12, 14, 15, 18, 19, 21, 23, 24, 26, 28, a1), (13, 16, 17, 20, 22, 25, 27, 29, 30, a2), (7-30, d)
                  COV = EXT*INT
                 ')
mod.anch <- multipleGroup(items, model=model.syntax, group=cohort, invariance=c('free_means', 'free_var'), method = 'MHRM')

Everything runs smoothly, but I get an error when I try to plot anything from the model object (I'm particularly interested in having a look at the trace lines):
> plot(mod.anch, type='trace')

I've talked to Matthias about this, and in mirt this seems very unlikely. Optimizing the M-step in particular would be very ineffective because of mirt's use of R's optimizers, which only run on single cores. Plus, the customized IRT models that can be written would be extremely painful to parallelize because the code is written in pure R rather than compiled code.

I think if I were to write a different version of the package, possibly in a language like Julia, then this type of customization would seem more plausible.

Phil
